/cases/1/reviews?profile=demo.summary: Strongest on narrative and on technical feasibility. Weakest on risk: the case names risks in prose but never sizes them, and there is no stated point at which the programme would be stopped.

scores.comment: Sources are named and ranges are honest, which is more than most cases manage. Marked down because the three weakest assumptions carry the most weight, and because the 707k gap between the bottom-up total and the claimed 4.2M is displayed but never explained.

Correctly identifies this as a forecasting and optimisation problem rather than an LLM one, and says so despite the director asking for AI. Data gaps are named as gaps. Loses points for treating product master quality as a risk rather than investigating it before committing to a build estimate.

Run costs, licences and change management are all present, which is unusual and creditable. Undermined by benefit_stockout, whose 2.3 point improvement comes from an unrelated sector, and by benefit_planner_time, which is not cash.

challenges.challenge: Seventy-two thousand euros of "planner time released" is not a saving. Nobody leaves, no overtime budget is cut, and the four planners will fill the time. Remove it from the base case or show me the signed commitment to reduce the overtime budget by that amount.
challenges.evidence_demanded: A written commitment from operations to cut the overtime budget, or the line comes out.

challenges.challenge: Four planners have run this on their own spreadsheet for years. Your plan tells them what to order and asks them to approve it. If they do not trust the first month of proposals they will override every one and you will have built an expensive suggestion box. Where do they appear in your plan before go-live?
challenges.evidence_demanded: A design that has the planners building the safety stock logic with you, not receiving it.

challenges.challenge: The whole case turns on the stock-out rate falling from 6.1% to 4.5%. That number comes from a vendor case study in a different sector with different demand volatility. What does it look like at half that improvement?
challenges.evidence_demanded: Either a backtest of the forecast on your own 36 months of history, or the base case rebuilt on a 1 point improvement.

challenges.challenge: Your tree adds up to 3.49 million. The director said 4.2. You have shown me the gap without explaining it. Either the director's number is wrong, in which case say so, or you are missing 700 thousand euros of causes.
challenges.evidence_demanded: Where the remaining 707k sits, or a statement that it does not exist.

challenges.challenge: Shortage reasons are free text and the portal does not record abandoned orders at all. You have listed both as gaps to close "before build" without costing either. Making a field mandatory at pick confirmation is a WMS change, a training exercise and a month of dirty data. Where is that in the 480 thousand?
challenges.evidence_demanded: A costed data remediation line in the ROI model.

challenges.challenge: You have attributed every overtime hour in the planning and depot supervision population to replanning. My supervisors do stock counts, customer escalations and shift cover with those hours. That figure is inflated and you know it — you wrote as much in the rationale.
challenges.evidence_demanded: A two-week time sample, split by activity.

challenges.challenge: One point one FTE to run a forecasting service, two models, a lakehouse and a semantic layer, in an organisation with no data engineers today. That is the run cost of a team that already knows the platform, not of the first one.
challenges.evidence_demanded: Run cost benchmarked against a first-platform organisation.

challenges.challenge: The pilot has a success definition and no failure definition. What result at month four stops this?
challenges.evidence_demanded: A stated kill criterion with a threshold.

/cases/1?profile=demo&scenario=base.symptom: The commercial director states that stock-outs and emergency logistics cost the company about 4.2 million euros a year, and wants "AI" applied to it. No breakdown of that figure exists and nobody in the room could say where it came from.
/cases/1?profile=demo&scenario=base.company_context: Regional beverage distributor, six depots, roughly 2,400 active SKUs and 380 employees. Orders arrive through field sales and a small B2B portal. Replenishment is decided weekly by four planners working from ERP reports exported to Excel. There is no forecasting system; safety stock levels were last reviewed in 2023 and are held as static ERP fields.

reconciliation.verdict: The tree explains 3,492,608 of a claimed 4,200,000. 707,392 (16.8%) is unaccounted for: either causes are missing, or the claimed figure is wrong and should be challenged.

solution.data_requirements: Order line history with shortage flags (ERP, 36 months); stock movements and expiry dates by depot (WMS); supplier confirmed versus actual delivery dates (ERP purchasing); carrier invoices with lane and urgency flag; product master with shelf life. Two gaps must be closed before build: shortage reasons are free text and need a controlled vocabulary, and the portal does not currently record orders abandoned for lack of stock at all.
solution.architecture: Incremental extraction from ERP and WMS into partitioned Parquet in a lakehouse, silver layer conformed on product and depot, gold layer as a star schema on order line fact and stock movement fact. Forecasting and allocation run as scheduled jobs against the gold layer. Power BI semantic model on top for planners and the commercial director.
solution.ai_component: Two models, neither of them large. A weekly SKU-depot demand forecast (gradient boosting on lagged demand, price, seasonality and promotion calendar), and a stochastic safety stock calculation driven by forecast error and observed supplier lead time distribution. An allocation heuristic weights remaining shelf life against forecast demand per depot. Explicitly not an LLM problem: the director asked for "AI", but the value here is forecasting and optimisation.
solution.automation_component: Replenishment proposals written back to ERP as draft purchase requests for planner approval, replacing the weekly Excel rebuild. Approval stays human — trust has to be earned before the loop is closed.
solution.process_change: Weekly planning becomes a review of exceptions rather than a rebuild. Safety stock parameters move from static ERP fields to a calculated table with a monthly review cadence. Shortage reason codes become mandatory at pick confirmation.
solution.governance: Named owner for the product master (currently nobody). Forecast accuracy and bias reviewed monthly in the existing S&OP meeting rather than in a new forum. Model retraining quarterly with a documented acceptance threshold; a model that fails it does not ship, and the previous version stays in service.
solution.deployment_plan: Two depots for the first four months, chosen for data quality rather than for size, with the other four as a comparison group so the benefit claim can actually be measured. Full rollout only if forecast accuracy and the stock-out rate both move in the pilot.
solution.key_risks: Product master quality is unknown and could delay the build by a quarter. Planner adoption is the largest risk: the Excel model is theirs and replacing it without their involvement will fail. Supplier lead time variability is partly commercial, not analytical, and no model fixes a supplier who is late by choice.

kpis.name: Order line fill rate
kpis.definition: Lines shipped complete on first attempt, divided by lines ordered.

kpis.name: Forecast accuracy (1 - weighted MAPE)
kpis.definition: At SKU-depot-week grain, weighted by volume.

kpis.name: Planner hours in weekly cycle
kpis.definition: Tracked to test the released-time benefit rather than assume it.

roi_models.notes: Benefits ramp at 50% in year 1 (two-depot pilot for four months, then rollout) and reach full run rate from year 2. Discount rate of 12% is the rate the group applies to internal projects.

reconciliation.verdict: The tree explains 2,307,400 of a claimed 4,200,000. 1,892,600 (45.1%) is unaccounted for: either causes are missing, or the claimed figure is wrong and should be challenged.

solution.data_requirements: Order line history with shortage flags (ERP, 36 months); stock movements and expiry dates by depot (WMS); supplier confirmed versus actual delivery dates (ERP purchasing); carrier invoices with lane and urgency flag; product master with shelf life. Two gaps must be closed before build: shortage reasons are free text and need a controlled vocabulary, and the portal does not currently record orders abandoned for lack of stock at all.
solution.architecture: Incremental extraction from ERP and WMS into partitioned Parquet in a lakehouse, silver layer conformed on product and depot, gold layer as a star schema on order line fact and stock movement fact. Forecasting and allocation run as scheduled jobs against the gold layer. Power BI semantic model on top for planners and the commercial director.
solution.ai_component: Two models, neither of them large. A weekly SKU-depot demand forecast (gradient boosting on lagged demand, price, seasonality and promotion calendar), and a stochastic safety stock calculation driven by forecast error and observed supplier lead time distribution. An allocation heuristic weights remaining shelf life against forecast demand per depot. Explicitly not an LLM problem: the director asked for "AI", but the value here is forecasting and optimisation.
solution.automation_component: Replenishment proposals written back to ERP as draft purchase requests for planner approval, replacing the weekly Excel rebuild. Approval stays human — trust has to be earned before the loop is closed.
solution.process_change: Weekly planning becomes a review of exceptions rather than a rebuild. Safety stock parameters move from static ERP fields to a calculated table with a monthly review cadence. Shortage reason codes become mandatory at pick confirmation.
solution.governance: Named owner for the product master (currently nobody). Forecast accuracy and bias reviewed monthly in the existing S&OP meeting rather than in a new forum. Model retraining quarterly with a documented acceptance threshold; a model that fails it does not ship, and the previous version stays in service.
solution.deployment_plan: Two depots for the first four months, chosen for data quality rather than for size, with the other four as a comparison group so the benefit claim can actually be measured. Full rollout only if forecast accuracy and the stock-out rate both move in the pilot.
solution.key_risks: Product master quality is unknown and could delay the build by a quarter. Planner adoption is the largest risk: the Excel model is theirs and replacing it without their involvement will fail. Supplier lead time variability is partly commercial, not analytical, and no model fixes a supplier who is late by choice.

challenges.evidence_demanded: A costed data remediation line in the ROI model.

challenges.challenge: You have attributed every overtime hour in the planning and depot supervision population to replanning. My supervisors do stock counts, customer escalations and shift cover with those hours. That figure is inflated and you know it — you wrote as much in the rationale.
challenges.evidence_demanded: A two-week time sample, split by activity.

challenges.challenge: One point one FTE to run a forecasting service, two models, a lakehouse and a semantic layer, in an organisation with no data engineers today. That is the run cost of a team that already knows the platform, not of the first one.
challenges.evidence_demanded: Run cost benchmarked against a first-platform organisation.

challenges.challenge: The pilot has a success definition and no failure definition. What result at month four stops this?
challenges.evidence_demanded: A stated kill criterion with a threshold.

/periodic-reviews?profile=demo.body_md:
**Shipped this quarter:** ERP-to-lakehouse ingestion project, one meetup
talk, one business case taken through review. Quota met on projects and
talks; article quota missed — zero published against a target of one.

**Stalled:** Fabric proof of concept opened 6 July, no commits since the
13th. Forecasting project has been in `planned` since February.

**At risk through decay:** operational KPI design, report design and
procurement are all past their decay window, and report design is still
claimed at level 3 with nothing published behind it since October 2024.
Statistics was downgraded from 3 to 2 in April and nothing has been done
since; it gates machine learning, forecasting and experiment design —
three skills the target roles all require.

**Against the market:** all three captured postings demand ROI modelling
or business case construction at level 4. Current level is 2. This is
the single largest gap in the profile and it is not a technical one.
/periodic-reviews?profile=demo.next_action: Take corporate finance and NPV to level 3 before opening another technical project.
/periodic-reviews?profile=demo.next_action_rationale: Both gate ROI modelling, which every target role demands at level 4 and which the review board scored lowest. Another pipeline project raises no skill that is currently blocking anything.

/phases.name: Foundations
/phases.objective: Convert an Excel and Power BI base into genuine data engineering foundations: SQL beyond querying, dimensional modelling, Python, the Azure and Fabric platform, and working literacy in models and agents. The measure of this phase is not exams passed but whether a complete pipeline from source to dashboard can be built unaided.

/phases.name: Technical reference
/phases.objective: Become the person locally who ships the whole chain — ERP to data platform to AI component to dashboard — and can defend every design choice in it. Local conference presence begins here, as does the first paid advisory work.

/phases.name: International reputation
/phases.objective: Move from locally known to externally cited: regular publication, open source with users other than yourself, international speaking, and engagements won on reputation rather than on application.

/phases.name: Authority
/phases.objective: Set direction rather than follow it: reference material others teach from, advisory work with large groups, and a practice that exists independently of any single engagement.

/skills/levels.name: Not started
/skills/levels.definition: No exposure. Cannot describe what the skill is for or when it applies.

/skills/levels.name: Aware
/skills/levels.definition: Can explain what it is, why it matters and roughly when to reach for it. Cannot yet apply it without a tutorial open.
/skills/levels.evidence_expectation: Reading or a course. Not sufficient to claim anything above this level.

/skills/levels.name: Applied with help
/skills/levels.definition: Has used it on a real task, following an example or with review. Produces correct results on well-shaped problems.
/skills/levels.evidence_expectation: A small project, an exercise repository, a guided implementation.

/skills/levels.name: Autonomous
/skills/levels.definition: Uses it unaided on real problems, including messy ones. Knows the common failure modes and can debug them. This is the working threshold: it is the default level required by graph edges.
/skills/levels.evidence_expectation: A shipped project where the skill was central, or a relevant certification backed by applied work.

/skills/levels.name: Designs with it
/skills/levels.definition: Makes architectural choices with it, judges trade-offs, and can justify those choices to a technical audience that disagrees.
/skills/levels.evidence_expectation: A production system, a published technical article going beyond usage into design, or a paid engagement.

/skills/levels.name: Authority
/skills/levels.definition: Teaches it, sets standards for others, and is sought out on it. Has an opinion on it that other practitioners cite.
/skills/levels.evidence_expectation: Conference talk, sustained open source contribution, published reference material, or repeated advisory engagements.
